newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Up to 40 said killed in Cambodia coup aftermath.
newsitem.headline: Up to 40 said killed in Cambodia coup aftermath.

text.p: Up to 40 Cambodians have been killed since the overthrow of the first prime minister but it was not clear if the killings were part of a planned purge, a diplomatic source said on Wednesday.

The source, who declined to be identified, said there was evidence of torture among some of the victims, including four bodyguards of First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh's top military commander, General Nhiek Bun Chhay.
The guards were found dead with their eyes gouged out.
"It's very unclear if this is a centrally orchestrated, carefully planned purge or more dispersed -- a general uncoordinated attack on FUNCINPEC officials," he said.
"But even if it is the latter, it could be stopped," the source said.

"Of course we are afraid. People are being arrested and some have been killed," a youth leader of the royalist FUNCINPEC party told Reuters as he and four other opposition activists were holed up in a small "safe house" in the capital.

The men are uncertain if their lives are actively at risk and Western rights workers with whom they have consulted have no clear idea either. Many other activists like them are also in hiding in Cambodia or have fled the country.
Second Prime Minister Hun Sen overthrew Ranariddh on July 6 after a weekend of fighting in the capital. Ranariddh left Cambodia a day before the coup.

In what political analysts see as a bid to legitimise his takeover, Hun Sen has said he wants to preserve the coalition between his Cambodian People's Party (CPP) and Ranariddh's FUNCINPEC party. He said he did not want the job of first prime minister and FUNCINPEC must choose a replacement for Ranariddh.
On Wednesday, Foreign Minister Ung Huot said he was willing to accept the job as Hun Sen's new coalition partner.
Ung Huot, a senior FUNCINPEC member, said he would keep his job as foreign minister.
"I accept to be first prime minister because I put the interests of my people and my country above everything else," Ung Huot told reporters.
"The interests of the country dictate that Cambodia must go on...We cannot wait," he said. "We've suffered too much."

An adviser to Hun Sen said the CPP accepted and would support Ung Huot's nomination while political analysts said the foreign minister's appointment would help the powerful second prime minister in his efforts to legitimise his new government.
"This is a real snow job. He (Hun Sen) is seeking legitimacy," said an Asian diplomat.
"(Ung Huot) is an ideal choice because he'll polish Hun Sen's image, nothing more, nothing less," said another diplomatic source. "He's a great face for the government ... (but) he's a stooge."
King Norodom Sihanouk, Ranariddh's father, on Tuesday said he was upset by reports that Hun Sen's forces had tortured and put to death opponents and urged an end to the bloodshed.

"I am profoundly distressed at the reports that the military and members of the national police have cruelly tortured and killed without mercy their enemies after having arrested or captured them," Sihanouk said in a letter sent from Beijing to Chea Sim, the acting head of state, in Phnom Penh.
Sihanouk was in Beijing for medical treatment at the time of the coup.

Hundreds of supporters and soldiers loyal to Ranariddh are believed to remain in detention but military officials have denied that detainees were being mistreated and said they were undergoing "re-education".

Hun Sen said on Tuesday Cambodia would have a free and fair election on May 23 as planned but the United States said that Hun Sen's rhetoric in recent days, seemingly in favour of democracy, was not matched by action.

"(Hun Sen's) words are beautiful over the past 48 hours ... but whether or not he can match those words in reality with his actions is a very big test for him," U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns told a news briefing on Tuesday.
Ranariddh has called for resistance to Hun Sen and appealed to the international community for support but he has so far received no firm offers of help.
